catholique" on march 17

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I wish to state that on March 17, 1942, L'Action Catholique published the following remarks about me:
While behaving like a choir-boy, Mr. Lacombe uses coarse language. . . .
Yesterday he said, without turning a hair, that the Quebec East electors had allowed themselves to be bribed wholesale because they did not vote for the Canadian party.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that this item is a pure fabrication. The hired scribe of L'Action Catholique would deserve to be summoned to the bar of the House of Commons to answer for his wanton attack against me and the Canadian party.
Mr. Lorenzo Pare would like to shelter under a racial cloak the alleged hero whose defence he takes. What he writes about me is a tissue of lies. The ineptitudes of that scribe are beneath my contempt.
Since it has allowed such foul statements to be published in its columns, I ask the readers of L'Action Catholique to return that paper to its editor, after having struck out the word "Catholique", which those people should no longer be permitted to besmirch. The fact that they are drawing money from the provincial treasury is their own concern. They are at liberty to wallow in the black ink of Mr. Godbout's printing contracts. Let them change the name of their paper or cease to publish it, because that is imperative in the best interests of religion and country. How shameful for a

Questions oj Privilege
paper bearing such a great name to ridicule the choir-boys who are both the adornment and the pride of our places of worship!

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
speechtext: How can a paper which bears such a great name attack a member who has for years stood up in this parliament in defence of our religion and our creed against the attacks of the Reverend Shields and the breakers of the Sabbath. What a servile attitude! What a disgrace!

maintopic: MR. POL'LIOT-REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF MR. RALSTON ON MARCH 5

speechtext:
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temisoouata): Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege, and I shall proceed by referring to some exhibits. Exhibit P-1 is the French text of a letter which I read in the house on March 2, and which is transcribed at page 953 of Hansard. I hold in my hand the very copy that was sent to Hansard, in which there is reference to "F. Lieutenant, Mr. Wisseman," though I learned afterwards that the real name was W'iseman. Exhibit P-2 is a copy of Hansard for March 2, in which I note something wrong in the translation of that letter. The translation does not mention that "F. Lieutenant Wisseman" was "F. Lieutenant." He is only called "Lieutenant Wisseman." Exhibit P-3 is a copy of Hansard of March 5 at which time, on the orders of the day, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) referred to my statement, which I have already mentioned, in these words, at page 1049:
During the course of that same speech the hon. member read a letter from some young man at a training camp at Brantford, complaining that he had been subjected to some persecution on account of speaking French, and that in the course of an altercation which
Questions oj Privilege

occurred he was arrested and put into the guard room. I have had a report from the training camp at Brantford, and the information I get is that a check of the guard reports reveals that only two men were confined in the guard room over the week-end of February 1, 1942, which was the date referred to, these being two drunks. Neither of these men was a French-Canadian. Inquiries made of all concerned reveal no knowledge of any such fracas as that described. There is no officer at this training centre by name of Lieutenant Wisserr.an, which is the name of the officer referred to by the hon. member in his speech.
There are many other exhibits which I cannot produce just now. They are copies of the five o'clock editions of the local newspapers on March 5, and the morning editions of March 6, in which the statement made by the minister in the house was quoted under big headlines. But on March 4, before the minister made his reference in the house, Mr. Malcolm MacLean, one of the assistants to the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), telephoned and asked for a copy of the letter, which I sent him. Then I received from the air department a report which was altogether different from that received from the Department of National Defence. All the facts I mentioned in the house were substantiated in the report that was sent to me by Mr. MacLean.
I congratulate the Minister of National Defence for Air on having transferred the man who lodged the complaint to another camp in the province of Quebec. But my first point is this. We have such difficulty in getting information at times, especially from the Department of National Defence, that when hon. members ask for definite information they should be given accurate information. My second point is that during this war all five war ministers are jointly responsible for all war departments, and no minister can give information of the kind given by the Minister of National Defence unless he obtains complete information beforehand. There are two camps in Brantford, one under the Department of National Defence and the other under the Department of National Defence for Air. My submission is that it was not right for the Minister of National Defence to answer the question as he did without first looking at the text of the letter I read, which was correctly quoted during the course of my speech as reported in Hansard, and second without knowing whether the complaint was about any camp in Brantford. Therefore, sir, I protest very strongly about it, and I hope such a thing will not occur again in future.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: MR. POL'LIOT-REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF MR. RALSTON ON MARCH 5
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend will look at his statement at page 1046 of Hansard he will see that he was referring
[Mr. Pouliot.l
to the handicap which he said sometimes existed with regard to French-Canadians in the army. He says, "French-Canadians are often handicapped in the army," and then he goes on, "Here is a letter that I will read." He speaks of the letter being in French, and then reads it. I saw a translation of the letter; I knew it was with regard to the army, and I made this statement. I made no inquiries whatever with regard to whether or not there was a training camp at Brantford under the Department of National Defence for Air; and I had no knowledge of there being any officer by the name of Wiseman there. I made the statement with regard to the army; and I think my hon. friend will realize that I and my colleagues are associated as members of the government, just the same as I am associated with my hon. friend the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and every other minister. Each minister must answer with regard to matters which may arise concerning his own jurisdiction, and I must say that I dissent from the suggestion that before answering a question with regard to the army I have to consult my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence for Air or the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services to find out if some particular incident occurred in connection with those sendees.

maintopic: MR. POL'LIOT-REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF MR. RALSTON ON MARCH 5

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES
subtopic: MEASURES TO ESTABLISH UNITY OF COMMAND IN RESPECT OF COASTAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement with respect to unity of command between the different services on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
The war committee of the cabinet have approved a unanimous recommendation from the chiefs of staff that the following measures be implemented at once with a view to establishing unity of command as between the three Canadian services in respect of the defence of the west coast of Canada, the east coast of Canada and Newfoundland:
(a)	The senior member of the joint service committee on the west and east coasts to be designated as commander-in-chief, west coast defences and east coast defences respectively.
(b)	The primary function of the commander-in-chief will be to coordinate the preparation and execution of the defence plans of the three services in respect of such forces as may be allotted to his command by the chiefs of the respective services. He will in consultation with the senior commanders of the other services, allocate tasks to the three services and coordinate the combined effort.
(c)	The commander-in-chief will exercise strategic direction of all three services and tactical command of his own service. He will not exercise tactical command in respect of any service other than his own. To ensure closer tactical coordination, the operations rooms of the three sen-ices on both coasts ire being combined.
(d)	The senior member of the joint service committee in Newfoundland will be designated, in respect of the three Canadian services, as commanding Newfoundland, defences. His functions in respect to Newfoundland will be the same as those kid down above for com-manders-in-chief, west or east coast defences.

speechtext: What steps have been taken by the government regarding the return to Japan of the Japanese minister in Canada, and likewise the return of all Japanese consuls and officials resident in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: JAPANESE MINISTER AND CONSULAR OFFICIALS IN CANADA
speechtext: The question of return to Japan of the Japanese diplomatic and consular officials resident in Canada is a counterpart of the question of return to Canada of the Canadian diplomatic and other officials resident in Japan and Japanese occupied territory in the far east. Their repatriation is also bound up with a general plan of exchange of United Kingdom and United States officials and officials of other allied countries. The consideration and discussion of conditions of exchange, under this general plan, by the allied governments concerned has been the subject matter of much correspondence between themselves and, through the representatives of their respective protecting powers, with Japan. Much progress has been made with a view to reaching a satisfactory agreement and to completing the necessary arrangements. The Canadian government has kept closely in touch with the situation, through consultation with the United Kingdom and the United States governments and through the government of Argentina, our protecting power in Japan and in conversations with the consul general of Spain in charge of Japanese interests in Canada. It may be added that, concurrently, consideration is also being given to the exchange of nationals who have no official status.

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide:-
1. That sums not exceeding one thousand million dollars ($1,000,000,000) be granted to his majesty towards defraying the expenditures that may be incurred during the present war for the purpose of enabling the government of the United Kingdom to purchase in Canada aircraft, tanks, mechanical transport vehicles, guns, ammunition and other munitions of war, foodstuffs, raw materials and any other commodities and supplies essentia] to the conduct of the war and the maintenance of the people of the United Kingdom, and to assist in

War Appropriation-Mr. Ilsley
enabling the government of the United Kingdom to defray other expenditures incurred in Canada for war purposes.
2.	That the Minister of Finance may be empowered to accept from the government of the United Kingdom an obligation of the said government in such form and subject to such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine for a sum of seven hundred million dollars ($700,000,000) in exchange for an equivalent amount, at an exchange rate of $4.45 to the pound sterling, of deposits in pounds sterling held in banks in the United Kingdom, the said obligation of the government of the United Kingdom not to bear interest until the termination of the war.
3.	That the governor in council be empowered to make provision for the purchase of any or all unmatured securities or obligations of or guaranteed, either as to principal or interest or both or as to dividends, by the Dominion of Canada or of or guaranteed either as to principal or interest or both by the Canadian National Railways, which are now or may hereafter be held by the government of the United Kingdom.
4.	That the governor in council be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, such sum or sums of money not exceeding in the whole the sum of one thousand million dollars ($1,000,000,000) as may be required for the purpose of defraying the expenditures and making the purchases referred to herein, the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I propose to make
a statement to the house on this resolution while Your Honour is in the chair. It was my intention to read the resolution, but it will shorten the time I have in which to make my remarks if I simply refer members of the house to it.
The purpose of the resolution is to secure authority to introduce a bill to implement the proposal for a revision of our financial relations with Britain which was outlined by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his address on the speech from the throne on January 26.
Before explaining the major provisions of the resolution and of the bill which will follow, I think it would be desirable for me to give a brief historical review of our financial relationships with the United Kingdom and the rest of the sterling area since the outbreak of war. By doing so, it will be possible for me not only to explain the methods which have been followed from time to time but also to give to the house the necessary statistical information to show the magnitude of the problem which has had to be met and the extent to which different forms of assistance have been relied upon.
As the house is aware, the British requirements of Canadian dollars to make payment for their large purchases of munitions and war implements, foodstuffs, minerals and other products have greatly exceeded the amount of Canadian dollars they have realized through their exports to Canada, through their receipts of interest and dividends and through other ordinary commercial transactions between the two countries. Even before the war, the British balance of payments with Canada resulted in a deficit of Canadian dollars. In 1939, for example-and the figures for that year were not materially different from those for 1938- our exports to the United Kingdom amounted to 1331 million, while our imports were only $113 million, leaving a British merchandise deficit with Canada of $218 million. The rest of the empire, too, exported to us less than they purchased from us; in 1939 our exports were $104 million and our imports $75 million. The empire as a whole, therefore, had a net merchandise deficit of $247 million with Canada in 1939.
The extent to which our industry and our agriculture have contributed toward furnishing our British allies with the sinews of war, in the form of foodstuffs and primary products as well as war implements of all types, is strikingly illustrated in the remarkable rise in our exports in 1940 and 1941. To the United Kingdom alone our shipments increased from $331 million in 1939 to $532 million in 1940 and $702 million in 1941. To the rest of the British empire, including Egypt, our shipments rose from $104 million in 1939 to $157 million in 1940 and $300 million in 1941.1 mention Egypt especially because it is now no secret that the mechanized equipment used in the Libya campaigns was to a very considerable extent produced by Canadian workmen in Canadian factories.
Our imports from the empire have been well sustained and the policy of the government has been to encourage them. But notwithstanding some increase in our imports, the empire as a whole had an aggregate merchandise deficit with Canada of $445 million in 1940 and $723 million in 1941.
Nor does this empire deficit of nearly $1,200 million on trade account in the past two years tell the whole story. In addition, large sums have been required for expenditures not reflected in the trade statistics. The most important of these have been the British capital investments in war plants in Canada, amounting at the end of 1941 to $238 million, and British expenditures in connection with
War Appropriation-Mr. Ilsley

air training activities in Canada. In addition, of course, there have been other expenses, such as for freight and storage, connected with the movement of goods within Canada.
Without going into exhaustive details, I may inform the house that after making allowance for all the sterling area's receipts of Canadian dollars of a current or ordinary nature-such as the proceeds of exports, interest and dividend receipts, shipping receipts and Canadian governmental expenditures in sterling incurred in connection with the maintenance of our troops in the United Kingdom-the sterling area's net deficit of Canadian dollars from the outbreak of war until the end of February, 1942, amounted to approximately 81,770 million.
This deficit has been financed in three ways. In increasing order of importance they are: gold payments from the United Kingdom to Canada; redemption or purchase, mainly in advance of maturity, of Canadian security obligations held in the United Kingdom; and the accumulation of sterling balances held by the foreign exchange control board on deposit in London.
Gold payments by the United Kingdom have amounted to 8250,000,000 over this whole period. As the house is aware, the last payment was received in December, 1940, and since that time the whole of the sterling area deficit has been financed by Canada out of its own resources. Over the period as a whole gold payments have covered less than 15 per cent of the sterling area deficit in Canada.
Not only have gold payments by the United Kingdom been kept to relatively modest proportions, but every ounce of gold we obtained from the United Kingdom was. promptly converted into United States funds and used to pay for United States goods needed to complete war orders for the United Kingdom. We cannot make the tanks, the anti-aircraft guns, the mechanized equipment of all sorts which we have supplied to our British allies, entirely out of our own domestic resources. We must purchase in the United States steel, machinery and machine tools, and coal and oil to drive the huge industrial plant which we have created and are still creating. For those things we must pay United States dollars. Exact statistics are not available, but there can be no doubt whatever that the amounts we have paid out in United States exchange in connection with British war orders in Canada are very greatly in excess of the amount of hard currency settlement received from the United Kingdom.
Our war production has, in fact, involved us in very heavy expenditures of American

dollars in the United States. Until December, 1940, the United Kingdom shared with us the burden of providing the necessary hard currency. Since then we have taken the whole burden on our own shoulders. The burden has not been a light one, in spite of the measures agreed upon at Hyde Park last April between the Prime Minister and President Roosevelt, which were calculated in part to alleviate our United States exchange difficulties.
I warned the house in introducing the budget last April that the need for United States exchange conservation had not passed; and lest anyone should think that the Hyde Park agreement has solved our United States dollar exchange problem, I should like to say that our official reserves of gold and United States dollars fell by S142,000,000, United States dollars, in 1941. Moreover, although the outlook is far from clear, it must be recognized that, failing remedial action, we appear to be faced with another sizable loss of reserves this year. Our United States dollar position is, therefore, still a major cause of concern. I stress this point because our United States dollar problem and our need of foreign exchange control are in part a direct consequence of our assistance to Great Britain, and it seems to me that at this time, when we are proposing to open a new chapter in our financial relations, the record regarding the past should be made quite clear.

The first of these, the 3i per cent dominion government loan of 1930/50, was announced in October, 1939, and was to an amount of over $90,000,000; the 4 per cent dominion government loan of 1940/60, the repatriation of which was announced in June, 1940, yielded $75,000,000; the third repatriation, that of the government-guaranteed Grand Trunk railway 4 per cent perpetual consolidated debenture stock, announced in October, 1940, yielded $105,000,000; and the fourth, the repatriation of the 4 per cent dominion government loan of 1953/58, the 3i per cent dominion government loan of 1958/63, announced in August, 1941, had to the end of February, 1942, yielded $130,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

That is $400,000,000 for the repatriation of government and railway securities. As I have explained to the house on a previous occasion, the principal way in which the British requirements of Canadian dollars have been met since December, 1940, has been through the foreign exchange control board buying sterling from the British exchange control authorities for Canadian dollars. By thus purchasing the sterling, Canadian dollars are made available to the British government for its purchases and other expenditures in Canada. The sterling purchased by us has been held on deposit in British banks to the credit of our foreign exchange control board, which of course acts as the agent of the government in these matters. These are the sterling balances to which I have made frequent references in the past, and the whole process has been popularly called the accumulation of sterling balances.
The amount of sterling held by the foreign exchange control board on deposit in London
has, of course, been reduced through the sale of sterling from time to time to the dominion government to purchase from the United Kingdom treasury the repatriated securities. After allowing for these and all other sales of sterling, including substantial sums used by the dominion government in maintaining our forces overseas, Canada's net accumulation of sterling balances from the outbreak of war to the end of February, 1942, has amounted to $992,000,000.
To summarize this part of my statement, the sterling area's deficit of Canadian dollars up to the end of February 1942 amounted to approximately $1,770,000,000, of which $250,000,000 was financed by the United Kingdom; nearly $125,000,000 was privately financed by discharge of private Canadian debts to the United Kingdom, including certain sales in the Canadian market of securities vested by the British treasury, and $1,400,000,000 directly financed by the dominion government-about $400,000,000 through repatriation of securities and nearly $1,000,000,000 through the accumulation of sterling balances in London.

The most striking feature of this table is, of course, the enormous magnitude of the recent Canadian dollar requirements of the sterling area. Its net cash deficiency, which amounted to $127 million from September, 1939, to the close of that fiscal year, rose to $668 million in the next fiscal year and it is estimated that it will approximate $1,075 million in the fiscal year now drawing to a close. Since December, 1940, the whole deficiency has been financed by Canada and practically the entire financing task has naturally fallen on the dominion government. We now estimate, it will be noted, that during the current fiscal year our own cash requirements for financing British war expenditures in Canada will be approximately of $1,029 million.
It is obvious that Britain's (and the sterling area's) purchases of foodstuffs, raw materials, munitions and war supplies in Canadia must continue, and probably increase. Canada has, indeed become an arsenal of democracy-after the United States and Britain the most important arsenal of democracy. The production of war supplies, including foodstuffs and war materials, and their supply to our allies, constitute one of the most important contributions which Canada can make to the winning of the war-to our own defence and security as well as to that of our allies. It would be unthinkable that any shortage of Canadian dollars should make it impossible, let us say, for Britain to secure from Canada the munitions and supplies necessary to equip and maintain her armed forces fighting on the front line, and the foodstuffs necessary to feed her gallant people. It was with this conviction that the Canadian government long ago advised the British Prime Minister that

the United Kingdom could continue to buy in Canada all essential supplies that could be procured and transported without any fear of her shortage of dollars-that somehow or another we would see that the Canadian dollars were made available. I believe that all Canadians approved the assurance thus given to the government of the United Kingdom. The enormous purchases and expenditures made in Canada by Britain and the rest of the sterling area have, of course, been an important factor in the expansion of production, employment and national income in this country.
The continuance of these purchases and expenditures, however, involves a continuance of the huge deficit of the sterling area in its balance of payments with Canada which must be financed (very largely at least, perhaps wholly) by Canada itself. We have realized for some time that the accumulation of sterling balances which, as I have explained, was the most important method of financing this deficit, was appropriate only as an interim or transitional form of financial assistance. It involved .the growing up of what was nominally a demand liability by Britain to Canada, the future of which was bound to involve uncertainties, particularly as the amount grew far beyond anything which could be repaid by Britain ia Canadian dollars except perhaps over a very long period of time. Moreover, the indefinite growth of this obligation, if permitted to continue for years, would have led to the existence after the war of what would be in effect a huge and unmanageable war debt owed by Britain to Canada.
I am sure that hon. members can recall the grave international problems and difficulties

War Appropriation-Mr. llsley
which arose in the nineteen-twenties and nineteen-thirties from the huge international war debts which had grown up during and immediately following the last great war. Here it is necessary to emphasize the distinction between a domestic debt and an international debt. Domestic debts involve payments between one person and another in the same country and give rise to no problems of currency and exchange. International debts, on the other hand, can be settled only by the transfer of goods and services from the debtor country to the creditor country. Such transfers can be made, only if and to the extent that the creditor country is prepared to accept goods and services from the debtor country for not only principal repayments but also annual interest charges. In other words, the creditor country must be prepared to see an increase in its imports or a decrease in its exports, or both. Experience has shown that countries will accept these payments in the form of imports only to a limited extent on balance, if at all. To do so, of course, exposes their producers to more intense competition from abroad, and the excess of imports serves as a deflationary influence which appears to be unwelcome in normal peace times. On the other hand, the inability of debtor nations to make payment when the creditor nation will not readily accept imported goods and services in payment, is bound to lead to international misunderstandings and frictions. Consequently, there is a practical limit to the amount of international debt which can be satisfactorily carried and repaid, particularly when such debt arises from the economically wasteful processes of war. The experiences of the last twenty-five years are too well known for me to labour this point at greater length.
With these considerations in mind, and believing that it was the desire of the Canadian people to do their utmost to contribute to the success of the common cause, the government felt that Canada should not continue to accumulate these financial claims against Britain at the rapid rate at which these claims have accumulated in the past twelve months. We believed that the existing shortterm and relatively informal interim obligations in the form of sterling balances, should be converted into a formal long-term loan, to the extent to which they could not immediately be used to redeem or purchase dominion government or Canadian National railway bonds owned by British investors. This would clarify the existing situation and remove any uncertainty as to the disposition of the large amounts of sterling balances which have been standing to Canada's credit in London. This, of course, would not result in any change in
the balance of indebtedness between Canada and Britain, but would be merely a change in form, with some offsetting of one claim against another.
In order to prevent the further rapid accumulation of sterling balances, the government believed that the best course to follow was to make an outright gift to Britain of the foodstuffs, raw materials, planes, tanks, guns and other war supplies which we would send to her, up to the value of $1,000 million. Of course, we shall continue to receive some goods and sendees from Britain which will automatically make available to her a certain supply of Canadian dollars or otherwise reduce her deficit with us. In other words, she will have receipts arising out of her ordinary exports to Canada, the shipping and insurance services she renders, interest and dividends on certain Canadian securities which will still be held by British investors, and the expenditures which we shall be required to make on our own armed forces in Britain.
Thus funds received in the normal way will meet part of the cost of British purchases and expenditures in Canada, and the $1,000 million dollar gift will be used in meeting the remainder of Britain's bills here; that is, in meeting what I have referred to earlier as the Canadian dollar deficit of the sterling area. This deficit of course arises almost entirely from Britain's requirements for foodstuffs, raw materials, munitions and other war supplies purchased here, so that the proposed gift will, in effect, take the form of these war supplies.
The explanation I have just given has been in very general terms. Perhaps I can make the matter clearer to the house if I now attempt to explain the more important provisions of the bill which this resolution seeks authority to introduce. In essence, the proposals are simple and straightforward; but because of the number and nature of the various transactions involved, and perhaps also because they deal in part with matters of exchange, which is a mystery to many persons, the details and perhaps the bill itself may appear complicated to many members of the house.
Let me state first that to-day the dominion is holding sterling balances to the value of approximately $1,070,000,000, at the current mid-rate of exchange, namely $4,45 to the pound sterling. By the time the bill has been enacted this amount will be somewhat larger, but it will, I think, conduce to clarity in our discussions if we take to-day's figures of our sterling holdings as the basis of our discussions. Sections 4 and 5 of the bill will provide in effect that approximately $1,000 million worth of these balances may be used for two

War Appropriation-Mr. Ilsley
purposes: first, an amount equivalent to $700 million will be transferred back to the British government in exchange for a British government obligation to pay $700 million Canadian dollars; and, second, a further amount will be used to purchase Dominion of Canada or Canadian National railway securities formerly held by British investors, but recently vested by the British government. The first of these provisions, it will be noted, merely provides for the conversion of sterling balances into a Canadian dollar obligation of the British government. This obligation will be non-interest bearing until the termination of the war, and thereafter the two governments will agree as to the rate of interest and other terms that will be applicable from that time forward. It has also been proposed to the British government, and they have agreed, that the funds arising from any redemption or repayment during the war of Canadian securities owned in Britain will be applied to the reduction of the loan-

Yes-as well as the proceeds of any sales to persons outside the United Kingdom of Canadian dollar securities now owned by residents of the United Kingdom. This will automatically result in a reduction of Britain's debt to Canada, at the same time that Canadian debts to Britain are reduced by the types of transaction I have mentioned. [DOT] The second provision involves simply another case of what I have called an official repatriation operation. This time we shall repatriate all the remaining dominion government and Canadian National railway securities still held in Britain, which are estimated to have a value of approximately $295 million. In this connection I may point out that these securities have been vested at the current market prices prevailing just before the public announcement of the proposals, namely on January 26 of this year.
It will be noted that these two provisions will use up nearly all the sterling balances standing to our credit at the time the bill will become law. I shall refer a little later to what we intend to do with the remaining amount of the sterling balances standing to our credit.
So much for the refinancing of past transactions which is to be accomplished by sections 4 and 5 of the bill. The main provision, of course, relates to the future, and is found in section 3 of the bill, which simply empowers the Minister of Finance, subject to regulations to be made by the governor in council, to pay to the British government lMr. Ilsley.]
out of the consolidated revenue fund sums of money up to an aggregate of $1,000 million to enable the British government to purchase in Canada foodstuffs, raw materials, munitions and other war supplies, and to defray other expenses incurred in Canada arising out of the war. Under the regulations to be approved, the Minister of Finance may make payments or advances from time to time upon his being satisfied that the amount thereof is necessary to make the said purchases and defray the said expenditures.
I can now say that it is our purpose, and the bill will so provide, that any sterling balances which are not required for the current operations of the foreign exchange control board after the provisions of sections 4 and 5 of the bill already referred to have been carried out, will be transferred to Britain and the dpllar equivalent thereof will be charged to this appropriation of $1,000 million. In this way all the sterling balances except those necessary for the current working purposes of the foreign exchange control board will be used up, and the gift will, in effect, begin sometime early this month, earlier than to-day. Until the exact amount of the securities to be repatriated has been determined it will be impossible to say what will be the amount of this excess sterling which will be handled in this way, but if our estimate of $295 million, representing the value of the securities to be repatriated, is correct, it will probably be of the order of $70 or $80 million.
The figure of a $1,000 million, representing the maximum amount of the gift to be provided for, was selected as being roughly the amount that would be necessary to meet the requirements of about a year's operations, on the basis of recent experience. If $70 or $80 million, as I have just estimated, is to be expended from the appropriation during the present fiscal year, the amount available for the new fiscal year will, of course, be $920 or $930 million. This should provide sufficient funds to take care of Britain's dollar deficit until sometime early in 1943. The house will,
I am sure, appreciate the difficulty of making a more precise estimate at this time. When the various sections of the bill are under consideration in committee of the whole, I shall be able to explain the various transactions which will be necessary with the foreign exchange control board to convert sterling balances into a Canadian dollar obligation of the British government, and to repatriate the dominion and Canadian National railway securities, but I believe that any attempt to explain these matters now might be needlessly confusing. I need only add that the bill will

War Appropriation-Mr. Ilsley
include the usual provisions found in any Canadian National railway financing and guarantee act enabling the government to make temporary loans to the Canadian National Railway Company in order to enable it to purchase its own securities, and that the concluding section of the bill will authorize the borrowing of moneys for the purposes of the bill up to an amount not exceeding $1,000 million.
When the repatriation operation has been completed and Britain has given its $700 million obligation to Canada in exchange for an equivalent amount of sterling balances, the balance of international indebtedness between Britain and Canada will remain on a reasonable and manageable basis. Britain will no longer hold any direct obligations of the Dominion of Canada or any securities of the Canadian National railway system, but she will continue to hold a considerable range of other Canadian securities and assets which will give her a continuing interest in Canadian prosperity. Included in these securities will be obligations expressed in Canadian dollars which I understand will amount in aggregate to roughly the same figure as the $700 million which Britain will owe to Canada in the form of the loan now proposed. That is the information I gave the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) a few moments ago. In addition, of course, Britain will hold a moderate amount of sterling obligations of Canadian debtors of various types other than dominion and the Canadian National Railways. The hon. gentleman asked me how much those were, or I undertook to tell him how much they were, and I said $300 million. I do not know, but we think it is in the neighbourhood of $300 million.

speechtext:
Oh, it could not be, in Canadian sterling obligations. *
I believe the house will agree that it is highly desirable that Britain should continue to have a financial interest in Canada and that Canada should continue to have a financial interest in Britain, rather than that we should attempt to cancel off all Canadian obligations to Britain against obligations to Canada. The mutual financial interest which will remain is bound to strengthen the other economic ties -between the two countries which have been of such great value to each in the past and will continue to be of great value in the future. The fact that both countries will now be creditors in relation
to one another as well as debtors reflects the developing economic maturity of Canada. Perhaps I should add that this developing maturity should carry with it a growing sense of responsibility-responsibility among other things to accept imports from abroad in substantial volume as a normal course of events.
The arrangements which are proposed in this resolution and which I have outlined, I hope in sufficient detail, will enable us to continue to implement the pledge we gave to Britain last year that she could continue to purchase what she needed in Canada for war purposes up to the limit of our capacity, and that we would see to it that the dollars she required for this purpose were made available. That pledge, and these new arrangements, are further instances of the way in which we are not allowing financial considerations to limit or interfere with our war effort either in regard to our own forces or in regard to the assistance we are giving to Britain. We are making finance adjust itself to the hard realities of the unlimited demands of war.
I should also mention that the arrangements proposed in this resolution do not alter the amount of money we must raise in Canada for war purposes. That is determined by the scope of our effort and not by the method of settling the accounts. Whether we lend the money to Britain, or give the goods to her, we must continue to find the funds to pay Canadian farmers, fishermen, lumbermen, miners and munitions workers who produce the goods. All that is really in question in this resolution, and the bill which will follow it is the means by which the accounts are to be settled-who is to be charged for them and what form the international balance sheet will take. Of course, these matters will be of importance in post-war times, and it is my belief that the plan now proposed is best calculated to satisfy our post-war needs and conditions.
I need not emphasize that the bill which this resolution precedes is one of first importance, and, indeed, one without real precedent. Its purpose is to enable Canada to make the fullest and most effective use of its material resources by feeding and equipping the people and armed forces of Britain in order that they may be able with us to win their fight and our fight against a ruthless and powerful foe who threatens to make this year, 1942, the most critical year in the history of civilization. The free and unconditional gift from the people of Canada to the people of Britain will express emphatically the will of the Canadian people to do everything in their power to help achieve victory and thus assure their survival and ours.

For generations before this war began Britain has been guarding our sea lanes and our trade routes and providing protection for our very existence, all without any cost to us. It has always been a matter of great regret to me that we have accepted this protection, in most cases without even an acknowledgment.
