Yes, like the machine gun matter. What kind of mentality does a minister of the crown possess who would at this of all times give expression to such a view? I hope the Minister of Finance will repudiate it. In the present position he owes it to himself, he owes it to the government of which he is a member, and he owes it to Canada and to all Canadians to repudiate such views. I do not for a moment suggest that the Minister of Fisheries was expressing the views of the government or expounding government policies. I should be astonished beyond measure if that were so. But I have never seen anywhere that the Prime Minister has repudiated these views or utterances of the minister, as reported in a reputable press agency of this country, and I call upon the Minister of Finance and the government to repudiate them. I call to mind a somewhat similar situation in the time of Sir Wilfrid Laurier when the Hon. J. Israel Tarte, taking advantage of Sir Wilfrid's absence from the country to attend a conference overseas, went about Canada enunciating doctrines at variance, on paper at least, although not in reality, with government policy. What happened to him? Well, he was just sacked-that is what happened to him, and that is what ought to happen to the Minister of Fisheries if he said what is reported is true.
In the Royal Bank review of March, reference is made to what is termed a "misunderstanding" which appears to have arisen about this proposal of the government, a misunderstanding which I personally had not been aware of, since I had not seen any adverse criticism of the proposal or any evidence of a misunderstanding. 1 made some inquiries and I presume there may be such by the man on the street who is questioning this transaction, who may think that if we give a billion dollars to Britain we shall have just that much less to spend in Canada. But as I understand it, and as the minister I think has made abundantly clear this afternoon, that is not the proposal. The government is asking the Canadian people, through parliament, to make provision for meeting Britain's shortage of Canadian dollars by supplying, free of charge and without obligation, to Britain, not money, but munitions of war, raw materials and foodstuffs, up to a total amount of one billion dollars.
We must realize that these munitions, raw materials and foodstuffs are in fact part of our own defence. The term "one billion dollars" is only a convenient way of expressing the total of these munitions, raw materials and foodstuffs which we shall send overseas. That money, the public should understand, will all be spent in Canada, for wages and salaries, raw materials, company earnings, and what not. Much of it, I venture to think, will find its way back into the public treasury and into the coffers of the provinces and municipalities in the form of taxation. So that perhaps it is not quite as much as at first it would appear. That, of course, is just an incidence of the expenditure.
In the first two years of this war we shipped to Britain goods, supplies, and munitions of war in excess of one billion dollars. Payment was made by Britain in several ways, the three most important being (a) shipments of gold to Canada; (b) shipments of goods exported to Canada, and certain services, shipping and the like, the collection of interest and dividends, which are usually termed services, I think; and (c) the repatriation of Canadian government and government guaranteed securities.
But a large portion of it, as stated here this afternoon in exact terms, is supplied, as I understand it, by Canada by lending the money to Britain with the resulting accumulation of sterling by Canada. The effect of the two operations is not greatly dissimilar, for the time being at least. In neither case are we sending actual money. It is retained in Canada and gives employment to Canadians. But, as the minister has pointed out, the real difference will be apparent in the post-war period when the problem of final settlement of all war debts will arise. I think it is reasonably certain that, if the war goes on long enough-and it looks as though it would- Britain will not be able to pay her debit *balances to us. Presumably her only means of payment would be in gold, goods and services. Payment in gold is most unlikely, I think, from now on. I doubt if She will have any to send us; for doubtless her gold will be exhausted by requirements in other quarters. I doubt if we shall want the gold) anyway,

1428	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mr. Hanson (York- Sunbury)
except to use it in the way the minister has indicated the gold has already been used, namely, for shipment out of the country in exchange for commodities in the United States. If we accept payment in goods, is that going to affect our post-war economy? This is a question which we must look squarely in the face.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: It depends on what kind of goods they are.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
Of course I agree that it depends on what kind, of goods they are. We must visualize the acceptance of some goods-I am willing to go with the the minister that far. Rut just how far can we go, having regard to the preservation of our own economy? I know there are Utopians who think that we are going to have the millenium with regard to trade after the war, and they interpret the Atlantic charter as the first step towards utopia. Let me again point out what I mentioned here a short time ago, that a very high authority in Britain, at the time we were over there, charged with this question of rehabilitation, and discussing .this very matter with us, told us definitely, referring to the Atlantic charter, that when the time came every country would have its own interpretation of that charter. That is the situation which we must visualize.
I return to my previous question: how is it going to affect our post-war economy? I ask it only for the purpose of stimulating thought, because we must have some thought for the future. At that time we shall be endeavouring to transform our war economy into a peace-time programme of employment for our own people-I mean our returned soldiers and sailors and our civilian population. That is the duty which will be cast upon the doorstep of this or some other government. We might as well ask ourselves right here, are we going to accept goods from Germany made under starvation conditions, perhaps on a fourteen-hour day basis-because that is what may happen if the German nation survives- ini competition with goods produced by Canadian workmen? I leave the matter there.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: We did, after the last war.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
Well, if we did after the last war, perhaps we can profit and benefit by experience. I am not going to take any decided position, because possibly I shall not have any responsibility in regard to it. But I ask the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald), in whose town are being manufactured certain goods with which these imports might come into competition. I ask the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martii ) 
who also lives in a community whose products may be in competition with those of the war-torn nations of Europe, nations which will want to live after this war is over, which will probably have to buy our food, and which may be producing under economic conditions and living standards which no Canadian would want to tolerate for himself or his people. At the moment I do not know the solution of the problem, nor do I attempt to give any.
I talked to a great industrialist in Canada about this problem not many months ago. We were speaking about the prospects of exports of Canadian-manufactured goods-not food products-and he said that he saw no daylight in the outlook for sales of our industrial products, which would meet immediate competition from continental Europe.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Some industrialists are getting ready right now for that very fight.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
We ought to take some long view in this matter. Certainly industrialists do not visualize any great happiness in connection with the export of industrial production from this country or the United States, countries whose standard of living is relatively high, in competition with countries in which there is bound to be a very low standard of living after the war. Of course if we are to have a system of communism-I do not use that word in its political sense-if we are to have a socialistic state where all will be at the same level, the Canadian workman may look forward to being dragged down to that level, not carried up to a higher standard. When peace comes we shall be faced with the problem of transforming our war economy to a peace-time programme of employment for our returned soldiers, sailors and airmen and for our civilian population theretofore employed in war work; and of reestablishing our industries on a peace-time basis, and of building up our domestic markets for consumer goods and finding markets abroad for our farm products and for such portions of our industrial output as we have available for export.
We do not want, I agree, to see a repetition of the position which obtained after the last great war, when international balances grew to dimensions which could not be dealt with, and when moratoria had to be declared. I should like to state this, however, that Great Britain certainly took care of her debt to Canada, and without any pressure at all.
This gift of one billion dollars, not in cash but in kind, and in the manner indicated by the minister-details of which we shall examine

War Appropriation-Mr. Coldwell
further when the bill is before the committee of the whole-is not only a great contribution to the winning of the war but it will, I believe, be some contribution to the winning of peace.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
I wish to say just a few words this afternoon, for I think it is necessary to read very carefully the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. llsley) in introducing this resolution this afternoon before making any extended comment upon what he has said.
I want first of all to congratulate him upon the clarity with which the statement was made, and to say that as I listened to him I thought it was one of the most interesting and probably most significant statements that has ever been made in this house. I say that because I think there was for the first time a clear recognition that, after all, all the economic obligations among nations are settled by exchanges of goods and services, and that while figures in the ledger may signify some things, money as we have known it does not enter into the transaction at all. Consequently we have to think, at the present time and in the post-war years, in terms of goods and services not money.
Speaking on behalf of the group with which I am associated, I want to say that we support this gift to Great Britain. We are, however, under no illusions. Had we had any illusions as to the idealism that seemed to lie behind this gift, I think the words of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) this afternoon will have torn them all from us. We are making this gift not only because we want to do something to assist in maintaining the morale of Great Britain and the winning of the war, but because under a capitalist economy we dare not allow our best customer to get into our debt. In other words, we have the paradox of capitalistic society outlined very clearly this afternoon, and we need not be hypocritical in thinking we are doing this entirely from altruistic motives. We are not.
I once heard a former leader of the opposition-I refer to the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett -say that when negotiating with the representatives of British business it was well to remember that they are quite hard-boiled. I was born over there; I lived there the first twenty-one years of my life; I know something of them, and I know the history of the country in which I was bom. I thoroughly agree with what Viscount Bennett said when he was leader of the opposition. I think that by the same token we should view this matter realistically and not obscure the real issues that are behind this gift by all kinds of platitudinous statements about our obligations and our patriotism.
One reason why I support this gift is that I want to see assistance given to the hard-pressed British people. When I was over there last autumn I saw something of their difficulties, some of their privations. But at the same time I want to keep clearly in my mind that in this parliament I represent the Canadian people, or a fraction of them, and I want to view this matter realistically from the Canadian point of view.
The Minister of Finance said in the course of his remarks that if we make this gift and do not receive securities from Great Britain by way of repatriation, it will give her a continuing interest in Canadian prosperity. That is a fairly realistic statement, and I agree with it, that so long as interest and dividends continue to flow from Canada to Great Britain, so long will certain people in Great Britain be interested in commercial relationships with us. But it is precisely that kind of thing which, after the war, I should like to see removed from our relationship with Great Britain, and removed from the world, for that is neither more nor less than hard-boiled economic imperialism. If we are going to consider these matters from the point of view of hard-boiled commercial economics, then we should try to view the whole picture in its proper setting.
I must confess I was surprised this afternoon when, in reply to a question which I asked, the Minister of Finance indicated that to-day the holdings of British investors in this country have been reduced to approximately $1,000 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: I may be wrong in that, sterling; that is the result of'my inquiries.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Well, as the leader of the opposition said, when we are discussing balances, what are seventy, or eighty or a hundred millions between friends? I was surprised, I must confess, to hear that the amount had been reduced so substantially. I brought down with me this afternoon a copy of the "Canadian Balance of International Payments", published in 1939. Speaking again in round figures, I find that in 1937, the last year recorded here, the balance of British investments in Canada was approximately $2,500 million. Therefore, since the war broke out, the amount has been reduced by approximately $1,500 million. I am glad that that reduction has been made, for while these interest and dividend payments are made to Great Britain, they go to only a very small class in Britain who own the securities upon which they are paid.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
All that is involved is a change of ownership.

War Appropriation-Mr. Coldwell

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: The goods and services which are exported from this country are the product of the toil and labour of the Canadian people, and consequently there is a lien, if you will, upon the labour of the Canadian people from outside this country.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
That is economic
nationalism.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: It is nothing of the kind.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: It is the worst type of it.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
Nothing of the kind. If economic nationalism means that the people of a nation are going to own their own resources, utilize them for the raising of their own standards of living and the satisfaction of their own needs, both national and international, then of course that is economic nationalism. But if the only basis of trade between nations is going to be between some great creditor nation and a large number of debtor nations, then we have most of the nations in the world held in slavery to one nation. That is the antithesis of freedom, the antithesis of liberalism and the antithesis of the right kind of human relationships.
At this point I should like to ask the minister to tell the house-not now, but at some future time-just what our economic position is in relation to the United States and what effect the war is having upon that relationship.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
What about Canadian
investments abroad, in other countries?

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: If nations in which we have made investments can, by the production of goods and services, pay them off, then to that extent those nations are or should be better off internally.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: No more free enterprise.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: "No more free enterprise," someone murmurs. That is analogous to the statement made earlier this afternoon, that socialism meant a dead level of equality. Well, of course, anyone who makes that statement is crassly ignorant of modern conditions.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I object to the use of the words "crassly ignorant," and ask that they be withdrawn.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: If the reference by the hon. member was to the leader of the opposition, I would ask that the remark be withdrawn.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: I will withdraw the word "crassly".

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: That is not good enough. The hon. gentleman should not attribute ignorance to me or any other hon. member.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: I will say this, then, that the hon. gentleman appeared to me to be ignorant of modern conditions.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: I think that should be withdrawn too.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
I need not withdraw that, because I am giving my opinion of the statement of the leader of the opposition; and I am not going to withdraw a warranted expression of opinion. To-day we have nations at war. We have Germany, which prostituted some of the features of socialism and called it national socialism; and even a prostituted socialism built up an economy which is causing us great trouble to-day. On the other hand, we have another nation with another theory called communism, which built up its form of socialism under conditions with which I profoundly disagree; but the basis was planning. The basis was the control and utilization of the economic resources and labour of those nations. To-day, whether we like it or not, we have to admit that they did a remarkable job in a short space of time. The challenge to us in the democratic countries is that if we are to survive under our democratic institutions, we must plan our internal economies so that men and women may live, produce, increase their standards of living after the war, and carry through the great war effort in which we are at present engaged.
But I was rather deflected from what I intended to say. I said1 I was surprised at the amount of securities already repatriated in Canada. In 1937, as I understood it, government securities including dominion, provincial and municipal securities, held in Great Britain amounted to $514,000,000; railway securities to $1,065,000,000, and manufacturing, mining and other securities to $1,105,000,000.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Are the interest payments given?

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
They are given, but I did not note them. On the other hand, Canadian investments in Great Britain amounted to approximately $41,000,000, or an amount almost negligible when considering the large sums with which we are dealing to-day. I was particularly interested in a break-down of some of these figures. Referring to page 25 of the document I mentioned previously, and using the last available figures for 1936, we find that bonds and debentures totalled some $841,000,000, less the estimated purchase back of $100,600,000, or a net of $140,500,000. That $841,000,000 was made up as follows: Canadian

War Appropriation-Mr. Coldwell
National Railways, guaranteed, $406,000,000; Canadian National Railways, not guaranteed, $107,000,000, or a total of $513,000,000. Canadian Pacific railway securities held in Great Britain were as follows; common stock, $175,000,000; preferred stock, $133,000,000, or a total of $308,000,000, and, in addition, debentures $288,000,000. That, as I say, was several years ago.
To-day the minister said that up to the end of 1941 we had already repatriated approximately $400,000,000 of securities, and that $295,000,000, or thereabouts, would be repatriated this year. In addition, if I heard him aright and got it down correctly, some private securities have been repatriated, amounting probably to another $125,000,000. Therefore the total repatriated up to date, and intended to be repatriated this year, will amount to $820,000,000. I want to get this quite clear, so that I understand it. The amount, therefore, that has been repatriated will be about $400,000,000. Was the $125,000,000 repatriated before the end of 1941? I was not quite clear on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Yes, up to the present.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: So the additional amount for this year will be $295,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: As I understand it, the Canadian Pacific railway stocks held in Great Britain, to the par value of about $308,000,000, and the debentures of the same company, amounting to some $288,000,000, or a total of about $596,600,000, have not been repatriated and are not being repatriated now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: The Canadian National obligations will have been repatriated at the end of the coming year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
I am not suggesting that this should be done in connection with this $1,000 million, but when we come to make a settlement, having made this gift, why not also consider the repatriation of the Canadian Pacific securities? Further, what is happening to these repatriated securities? What percentage of them is being held by the government; what percentage sold? If they are sold, all we are doing is replacing one set of investors with another set of investors. True, our own investors in this country will then own the repatriated securities, and henceforth interest payments will be made to people in Canada. But what we are actually doing is substituting the Canadian investor for the British investor and,
as the minister and the leader of the opposition both recognized, there may be some disadvantage in that from the point of view of trade and commerce, under our present economic structure.
I should like to see more of these securities, particularly of industries like-if and when we repatriate them-International Nickel, some of our power corporations and the Canadian Pacific Railway, held by the government, so that we might have a controlling interest in some of these organizations when the war ends. In the post-war years we are going to face serious problems of rehabilitation, and if we are to face them realistically, the control of some of our great resources and some of our great industries may be of fundamental interest to us. Therefore I should like to see a policy worked out in connection with repatriation plans whereby we would hold at least some of the securities so that we may have some determining voice in the control of Canadian industry when this war ends.
In conclusion, I should like to express this point of view once more-I felt it when I was in Great Britain; and others to whom I have listened since I came back, notably Mr. Brockington and others over the radio, have expressed the same opinion-that in Great Britain this is not only a war; it is something more than a war. It is the precursor of great social and economic change.
Only a few days ago I received a letter from a young man in Great Britain whom I met there, a young man who had been a member of a large elected body on which he sat as a Conservative. I sent over to him some of our literature, and the only criticism he made of that literature was this, that we were not going as far in our economic and social proposals as some of the younger men with whom he was associated in Great Britain were prepared and were determined to go.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Conservatives.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Yes, at present in the Conservative party, it is true. But they will have to leave the Conservative party in Great Britain, as others have had to do, before they are able to make any progress whatsoever; for to-day, I may tell my hon. friend, in my opinion the break-down we are seeing in the British empire is largely the result of blind, Tory policies pursued by reactionary governments of Great Britain.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
The
applause is from across the floor; there is the Tory party to-day.

War Appropriation-Mr. Coldwell

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
I did not refer to my hon. friends to the right as Tories. I referred to the Tories of Great Britain. But I am quite convinced of this, that our hon. friends to the right of Mr. Speaker are so close to the wall on the right that it is useless for our Conservative friends who sit to the left of Mr. Speaker to try to get between them and that wall; make no mistake about that.
But we have not yet apprehended aright what is going on. If we apprehend aright, we shall see that in our own country after this war we shall have to follow the world trend, and that world trend will be ever more and more in the direction of greater public control, public ownership-socialization, if you like the 'word better-

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Certainly not the way the government is operating its manufacturing plants.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
I do not think any government can operate a manufacturing plant; no government would ever attempt to do it. But the government of Canada could, as any other government can, hire just the same type of technicians, just the same brain, and they would act with even greater enthusiasm to carry on in the interests of the people rather than in the interests of the exploitation of the people. So I say that that does not frighten me a little bit.
I am very glad that this gift is being made. But let us view it realistically. We are prepared to give this to the British people, and we hope they will get it. We hope the British people will benefit from this, and not a few people in Great Britain. W'e hope that in the making of this gift it will ultimately benefit the people of Canada, too, not a few people in Canada-because otherwise the obligation which this involves may mean that there will be still $1,000 million worth of claims on the labour of the Canadian people for a very long time to come.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his speech the minister raised a number of interesting points which will no doubt raise many questions in the minds of hon. members. Those questions will have to be left over to the committee stage.
I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in his criticism of some of the statements made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). It is intolerable to feel that to-day we are fighting for a continuation of conditions such as existed in this country before the war, conditions which apparently the leader of the opposition feels must exist again at the end of this war. We have been told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie
TMr. R. B. Hanson.]
King) and by other members of the government that there will be a new social order at the end of the war. But judging from the statements made by the ministers themselves and by the leader of the opposition, it is quite evident they do not really believe there will be any fundamental change in future policies.
At the very outset I wish to say that the members of this group are whole-heartedly behind the government in the proposal to give to Great Britain outright a billion dollars' worth of goods. We feel that this should be regarded merely as a start of a new policy as between allied nations. It involves of course a completely new principle, and I am going to deal with that from two different angles. First I shall discuss the moral, and then the economic side.	'
Speaking first about the moral side, I think we will all agree that to-day there is only one real issue before this and every other one of the Allied Nations, and that is to defeat the enemy wherever he may be found, whether it be in Europe, in Asia, in Australia or in New Zealand. If we do not meet and defeat the enemy in those places we will eventually have to meet and defeat him on the North American continent. It is very important that the people of this country as a whole should meet that fact face to face, and more realistically. Unfortunately many people in this country still think that we can sit back on our doorsteps and wait for the enemy to appear. Let us constantly keep before our minds this allimportant fact, that the battle in Russia to-day is our battle, that the conflict raging in the Dutch East Indies is our conflict, and the same is true of Burma, China, Africa, wherever the enemy may be found. Let us realize this before we have to add America to the list.
I think it is apparent to everyone that the allies should cast every ounce of their strength against the enemy at this time. In order that this may be done it is very necessary that we should mobilize our maximum strength. I do not think we have done it up to the present time. I think I can show shortly that we in this country are a long way from having done that, and the same can be said of every one of our allies, including Britain. We should reduce all non-essential services down to the very minimum. We shall have to foe content to maintain a standard of living just barely sufficient to guarantee that our people can be maintained in a state of health and efficiency.
In my opinion the total available resources of all the allies should be pooled for a united effort under a united command. No matter where the battle may be, no matter in what part of this world we may have to fight, the total resources of all the allies should be avail-

War Appropriation-Mr. Quelch
able to a united command. This united command should be able to throw these total resources into the conflict disregarding completely who owned them before they were turned over. For example, let us assume that the united effort of Great Britain represents eight units; that of Canada four units; that of the United States ten units, and Russia twelve units. I am not suggesting for one moment that these figures represent a true comparison, I am just using them as examples. AH these units should be made available for a common effort against the enemy.
Would the United States be justified in saying that they are only prepared to put into that common pool eight of their units, but would sell the other two to any one of the more pressed nations? Apparently the minister thinks that there might be some justification for that, because he says we are giving a billion dollars to Great Britain and are having to find foreign exchange to buy from the United States. Personally I can see no justification for giving a billion dollars' worth of goods to Great Britain, on the one hand and, on the other hand, having to buy from the United States. This is just as much the war of the United States as it is the war of Canada, of Britain or of Russia. I cannot see any possible excuse for buying, on the one *hand and giving on the other. We should do everything in our power to convince the United States that this is just as much their war as it is ours, and therefore that they should be prepared to give to the common pool instead of lending.
As I was saying, at the present time apparently some people in Canada feel that we should give only one of our units and should lend or sell the rest. Again I say that the same thing that I referred to with regards to U.S.A. applies to Canada. I am reminded of an example which was drawn to my attention. Two men, one large and one small, were standing with their backs to the wall facing the enemy. The large man said to the small man, "I can fight a great deal better than you; I am going to put one of my hands behind my back and fight just with the other so we can put forth an equal effort. However, I will sell you the use of that arm in order that we can put up a better fight." Surely he should realize that unless he uses both arms, he as well as the other man will be licked. It is essential that he use both arms, whether or not he is able to sell them.
There should be no loans or sales as between the allied nations. Furthermore, at the end of the war, when the time comes for rehabilitating the devastated areas of the allies, that work should be done on the same basis, without loans or debts. If at the present time
better use can be made of our tanks in Great Britain, then those tanks should be given to Great Britain. If at the present time better use can be made of our tanks in Russia, then those tanks should be given to Russia. In order that such a proposal may be carried out in an equitable way it is essential that eveiy one of these nations should maintain their production at its maximum level and reduce non-essential services and be satisfied with a moderate standard of living. It would not be fair for one nation to say that it is going to have "business as usual" while the other nations cut down their expenditures to the very minimum. There must be an equality of sacrifice to the greatest degree possible.
Are we in Canada maintaining our production at the present time at its maximum level? I shall take one of the primary industries, that of agriculture. I know enough about agriculture to know that our production can be extended tremendously in many lines, such as poultry, hogs, honey, cheese, and so on. This can be done if the people are assured that they will get a price equal to the cost of production, and if the necessary organization is put into operation to produce this result. Unfortunately in this country to-day we are still thinking in terms of jobs instead of maximum production. Instead of organizing our production to its maximum, in order to provide jobs for people we are willing to allow certain non-essential services to continue. I have an important example of this before me which I should like to give to the house. I have before me a copy of the Financial Post of February 21. I should like to quote from page 17 to show how far some people are from understanding the real problem that faces this country. I quote:
Gold Fights for Canada
Canada's story is typical of that of other united nations. For Canada, gold provides:
1.	Foreign exchange-about $205 millions in 1941, equal to one-fourth of all the U.S. dollars provided by Canadian exports in that year, one-ninth of all Canada's exports.
I shall take one section of this at a time. If the United States were willing to let us have goods on the same basis as that on which we are giving them to England, it would not be necessary to export gold to the United States. That gold does not help the war effort of the United States in one single degree. If the United States are really interested in winning this war, would it not be better for them to say that they do not need this gold, that we should put our 32,000 miners, most of them skilled labourers, to work in war industries in order to expand our war effort? Paragraph 2 reads:

War Appropriation-Mr. Quelch
2. Taxes on approximately $60 millions of wages and salaries; on the $21 millions of supplies purchased; on the $94 millions left for direct taxes on mining profits, depreciation and dividends; on the personal income gained from roughly $50 millions paid in dividends by purely gold mining companies.
If those same men were put to work in war industries, would not the government be getting taxation from those war industries? Taxation derived from gold mining is no more valuable to the government than the same amount of taxation derived from war industries.
Paragraph 3 is the funniest part of it all. I cannot imagine that any person would be guilty at a time like this of making such a foolish statement. It reads:
3.	A living-for 32,000 miners, their families and the communities built up to serve them. Rough estimate of the total number supported by the gold mines has been placed at over
200,000	Canadians.
This publication contends that we should continue gold mining in order to provide jobs for 32,000 men; yet we are told in this house day after day that our production has reached its maximum capacity because we have not the skilled labour available. These men are mostly skilled machinists and miners; they are the type of men that are needed greatly to-day in our war effort. But apparently those with the gold mentality would rather go on mining gold, would rather keep these men working at some non-essential service that might handicap our war effort. I defy the minister or any one in this house to show me how these men are helping the united war effort of the allies in any degree whatsoever. If you leave the United States out of the war, yes, that might make it necessary for us to buy from them with gold. But with the United States in the war, you cannot say that gold helps in the slightest degree.
Paragraph 4 deals with morale. It says:
Gold production maintains the morale of the civilians.
To what extent would the morale of the people of this country be hurt if we stopped producing gold? On the contrary it would be raised considerably, because the people would realize that the government was waking up and at last cutting down on non-essential services. But the Financial Post says that gold production builds up the morale of the people.	Yes-the people who are getting
dividends from the gold mines. That is all that the Financial Post worries about

the shareholders. It goes on to say :
Many of those serving the miners could not find other jobs and would become reliefees instead of taxpayers if it were not for the steady production of the gold mines.

If these men were put into war industry they would not be out of work or -on relief. But is the government really interested in planning war production at this time? Do the words of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) mean nothing when they say that we are short of skilled labour? One wyould almost be led to believe so.
I want to refer briefly to a statement made by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette). I am sure -lie was perfectly sincere in what he said and I am not going to attack him on that basis. But I would point out that some of his arguments were not very sound. What he said was spoken in another debate during the present session and I cannot read it, but I shall briefly summarize some of his points. He asks us not to allow 65,000 people to be thrown out of employment by stopping the production of gold. I do not know where he got that 65,000. I thought it was around 60,000, but I wrote to the bureau of statistics and they assured me that the total number of men in all classes of the gold mining industry would not number more than between 32,000 and 33,000, with the exception of prospectors. But we w-ill use the hon. member's own figure of 65,000, because he -may include in that number the men who are providing food for the -miners. He said that he was not discussing the gold standard. He did not want to get into that argument. But what possible justification- can there be for supporting the production of gold unless at the same time you are prepared to support the gold standard? He urged that these men at work in the gold mines be not thrown out of work but be put on essential services. We are not urging that they be thrown out of work. There would be no sense in that. We are asking that the production of gold be stopped to release these men for essential services. The hon. -member for Cochrane seems to -think that we want to throw them out of work.
He also contended that if men should be kept on farms when there is a surplus of wheat, surely, therefore, gold mining should not be discontinued. He seemed to think we were inconsistent in wanting to keep men on the farms producing wheat not needed now, and at the same time condemning the gold mining industry. There again I point out that the number of men required to produce wheat is comparatively small. The part of agriculture that requires -the greatest proportion of labour is not the raising of wheat, but live stock and dairying, the products of which are very much needed to-day. One man may be running a one-section grain farm,

War Appropriation-Mr. Quelch
with an additional man to help at the harvest. My boy has been running a one and a quarter section farm, running the combine and engine himself, and the only help he has is a man to haul the grain away.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: He is doing better than his dad.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
He has better machinery than I had. On the other hand, just as soon as he started to go into live stock he had to have additional help. It is that which takes men for the farm. In the days of the old threshing machine we needed a lot of labour. It required ten men on a threshing gang. But to-day one man can handle what took ten men before the advent of modern machinery. Of course some members may say: If that is so, it cannot cost much to raise wheat. I do not want to leave that impression. It costs a great deal of money to buy that type of machinery, and the depreciation on it is very heavy indeed. That is where the money goes, to machinery companies, instead of to labour.
Another point. Even if the wheat is not urgently required, and I admit that it is not urgently required to-day, we realize that it is necessary to build up great reserves of wheat for the future. But even if it were not urgently required, that wheat at least is not harmful to anyone. No one would suggest that. On the other hand, large accumulations of gold are harmful because they give rise to an ever-growing demand on the part of certain people in high places that the country should go back to the gold standard. It would be a bold man who would say that the gold standard has not done tremendous harm to nations in the past.
I noticed a statement in a paper recently that gave me a great deal of concern. I raised the matter in the house this session, at page 60 of Hansard, as follows:
On January 21, 1942, there appeared in the Edmonton Journal an account of the scheme to be submitted to the Rio conference. Section 2 of the proposal, as outlined in the article reads:
"Creation of a free international exchange currency to facilitate flow of goods and prevent delay in transactions. It would be on a gold basis and in addition to the American nations, Great Britain, China, the Netherlands, India and all British dominions would enter into the agreement. A pool of allied gold holdings would be created. The Latin American countries would agree to peg their national currencies into the free international exchange currency."
I asked the Prime Minister whether or not Canada had any commitments, and he said that Canada had not any commitments, and that there has not been any correspondence on this matter. He did not state whether there
had been any discussions. I am satisfied that there have been discussions; there cannot be any doubt about that. I cannot believe that a statement such as the one I have just read would be submitted to the conference unless there was some foundation for it, and the statement says definitely, "Great Britain and all British dominions." Would that statement be made without any foundation? So that while the Prime Minister's statement that there has been no correspondence may be correct, I maintain that undoubtedly there have been discussions, if not on the part of the Prime Minister himself, at least by men in official positions. I shall refer to one of these gentlemen. I have here a copy of National Money News, published by the League for Economic Democracy. In its issue of January 15 at page 3, this item appears:
Doctor James going to Britain to discuss post-war plans.
Ottawa, January 13 (CP).-Doctor F. Cyril James, principal and vice-chancellor of McGill University, will go to Britain shortly to consult United Kingdom authorities on post-war reconstruction, officials at the Department of Pensions and National Health said to-day. Doctor James is chairman of the seven-man committee on reconstruction which acts as advisory committee to the federal cabinet.
Undoubtedly Doctor James has a definite official position in connection with post-war reconstruction. The dispatch goes on to quote from a statement that appeared in the Toronto Daily Star, which I have taken pains to verify, and here is the statement from the Toronto Daily Star of September 17, 1940:
That was an interesting speech to the American bar association at - Philadelphia by Doctor F. Cyril James, principal of McGill. The gold question, he declared, must be considered as a problem of social and political philosophy rather than one of pure monetary theory. If you believe in national isolation and autarchy, he said, the present gold policy of the United States is perhaps the most stupendous piece of folly in history. But if you believe in democratic capitalism and some kind of world economic order, it may be regarded as the most constructive contribution now being made, in any part of the world, to the future welfare of the United States and all mankind.
Doctor James used to be professor of finance at the Wharton school of finance and commerce at the university of Pennsylvania and is therefore an authority. He declared that the United States gold holdings-
This is the interesting point.
-now exceeding $21,000,000,000, were at stake in the war-
In other words, we are fighting to maintain the value of the $21,000,000,000 of gold holdings in the United States.



War Appropriation-Mr. Quelch
*-and that their value would depend on who won. A British victory meant continuance of gold as the monetary medium-
Mind you, this man, I take it, is speaking on behalf of the government. He is chairman of this seven-man committee. Otherwise he is talking out of turn.
-whereas a German victor}', as Doctor Funk himself recently made bluntly clear, would mean the setting up of regional autarchies in which gold would be useless except for economic decoration. Another definite reason, if any were required, for Canadians doing their utmost, in war loans and everything else, for the defeat of Germany! One of our greatest industries is gold mining and, to protect our economic order as well as our country and our homes, victory must be assured.
The whole speech is in defence of gold. He is chairman of this committee on post-war reconstruction. Therefore I do not doubt for one minute that there have been discussions. Maybe he is responsible for the statement made at the Rio conference.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: It is reconstruction on a gold basis.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Yes, it is reconstruction on a gold basis. I do not think there is any doubt of that. Anyone who reads the Financial Post to-day knows that they are continually harping on the fact that we shall be back to the gold standard after the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
The minister may shake
his head, but Doctor James is of the very definite opinion that that is the thing we are fighting for to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: I can tell the hon. member that Doctor James is not running the policies of this government.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: But he is chairman of the seven-man committee, acting in an advisory capacity to the government. It says so here. I suggest that it is high time the government got new advisers if they do not approve his advice. Why keep a man to advise you if you do not agree with his advice?

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: It may be window-dressing on the part of the government.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: If so, it is a very objectionable type of window-dressing, and not the kind of thing which is going to create the morale so necessary to the people of this country, or instil the will to victory.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: It is time to clean house.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Most definitely so.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: He represents one point of view on a committee which includes many points of view.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: But all representing the government point of view.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: I hope his point of view is only his own, but if the government have one man on the committee who represents that viewpoint, there is every reason to suppose that there are also others of the same opinion.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
The government
cannot control a man's speeches.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: If he, the chairman, was appointed by the dominion government, I think the government should have some control. A statement of that kind will be detrimental to the war effort. If the people get the idea that they are fighting to maintain our gold reserves and the interests of shareholders in gold mines, it is not going to have any good effect.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Let us call it a McGill university indiscretion.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
That is a very mild term.
There are many non-essential services, but I think this is the most glaring example of one which can be done away with without causing privation to anybody. Until we are rid of this kind of service I believe our war effort will fall far short of what it should be.
Another business which is in the same category is the liquor traffic. Does any one believe to-day that we could not very well ration liquor?

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: It depends on the man's capacity.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Would the hon. member suggest that if we rationed it, he would be any worse off physically than when he is allowed to drink an unlimited amount?

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: I do not drink. I am a teetotaller.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: I would suggest, joking apart, it would not hurt anyone for the duration of the war to be limited to, say a bottle of whisky a year.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: A week!

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: A day!

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
I understand some member to say that in British Columbia it has been reduced to one bottle a day. Perhaps the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) can give us some information in that regard.

Questions

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: STERLING AREA'S CASH DEFICIENCY OF CANADIAN DOLLARS
speechtext:
I do not want anyone to say that I advocate that the rum issue to the troops should be done away with. I do not suggest that for a moment. When men undergo what they have to undergo, a drop of rum makes a very great difference, at a time such as stand-to in the morning. But I do not believe that people in civil life need to be able to buy bottle after bottle week in and week out, and if their supply were curtailed severely it would mean not only a saving of labour but, I believe, an increase in efficiency. Last week-end I was in Montreal, and although I was there only one night I saw three brawls in the streets. They were caused by drunks, and when the policemen came up they just sat in their car and watched the fight. I am not casting any aspersions at Montreal; I do not doubt that similar scenes are taking place in many other cities.
We not only let down our allies but are false to ourselves when we do not put forward the maximum effort of which we are capable.
On motion of Mr. Quelch the debate was adj ourned.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, March 19, 1942
